utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, will you please have the witness brought in? (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters, the court reporters, counsel for the Prosecution, counsel for the Defence. I should like to remind us, for the benefit of the public, that we are in the cross-examination stage of the accused who is in the position of a witness under oath, and I shall give the floor to the Prosecutor as soon as General Blaskic has been made comfortable, whom I wish good morning to as well. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. Thank you very much. Good morning, General. Pursuant to your instructions or instructions of the registrar, Mr. President, if I could move back to those documents that we were ending with yesterday, and if we could just -- I split them up, as instructed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Registrar, can we have all these documents marked, please, in order?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit 609, 609A for the French version, 609B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, we're going to continue. I'll have them all marked, with the assistance of the usher at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges are giving their ruling regarding the request for a private session requested by the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think Mr. Harmon would like to provide some additional information on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we do that in private session, Mr. President? Could we discuss this issue in private session rather than have counsel or the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that it would be normal for the Judges to render their decision. The debate in principle was closed. But as the parties --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. We agree. We just prefer that the specific subject matter of our request be discussed in private session, not be addressed otherwise. Of course, if the Court can rule without identifying the specific request, that's fine, in public session, but if counsel has an argument, we would want that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you like us to have a private session just to hear your last remarks because the Chamber was on the point of making its ruling. We thought that we had finished the debate yesterday. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I just wish to add some additional information, Mr. President, to informations of the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But if you are adding, if you are adding any information, then, as requested by the Defence, please, we had better go into a private session. So a very short private session. I am saying this so that we do not lose the public. It has to do with an incident regarding a request of the Defence for a private, temporary session on which the Judges will render their decision. But we have a few more comments to hear before that, so we will do so in private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the court would have retired to deliberate, the registrar and I took the liberty of pre-marking some of the exhibits, and we now have a series of exhibits that reflect from Prosecutor's 609 to Prosecutor's 614 respectively. All of these documents, Mr. President and Your Honours, should be in B/C/S/, French, and English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibits 609, 610, 611, 612, 613, 614. For each of these exhibits there is a French and an English version. The French version being, for example, 609A and the English version being, for example, 609B. This is the case for each of the aforementioned exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecutor does not intend to read through all these documents, they speak for themselves, but if we reflect just briefly on each of the documents. The subject matter of these documents has to do with the killing of an individual by the name of Drazen Gvozden, that we can see from these documents was a member of the army of the Republic of Croatia. He was killed on the 3rd of October, 1993 in an area around Siroki Brijeg Herzegovina, and while he was killed, this soldier from the Republic of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Kehoe. You're talking about 610 or 609? 609 doesn't mention Mr. Gvozden. What document are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will take them in series. The first document, 609, is the judgement against Marinko Musa, who is a member of the HVO, who was accused of manslaughter in the killing of Drazen Gvozden. On the 9th of September of 1994 in the Mostar military Court, Mr. Musa was found not guilty of that charge. In the next document -- I might reflect that the judgement of the Court in 609 does reflect that Mr. Musa did, in fact, shoot and kill Mr. Gvozden, but for extenuating circumstances he was found not guilty of involuntary manslaughter. The next document, 610, is an HVO certificate of death concerning Mr. Gvozden which notes that Mr. Gvozden was killed in combat against Muslim armed forces on Hum near Mostar on 3 October, 1993. That, of course, is in contrast to the prior document where, in fact, Mr. Musa shot Mr. Gvozden. The next document, Mr. President, is a newspaper article which reflects the filing of a lawsuit by the Gvozden family against the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and it concerns the shooting death of Mr. Gvozden, and it notes at the outset, and I will direct the Court to the first line of 611, where it says: "Drazen Gvozden, a member of the Croatian Army from Sesvete, was killed on Mount Hum near Mostar in October 1993." This particular lawsuit was filed in Zagreb, and the document reflects via attorney Ranko Radovic, who was representing the Gvozden family, that part of this lawsuit was sent back to Mostar to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It notes in the second paragraph of this article that the lawsuit alleges that -- "the Gvozden family alleges that Drazen Gvozden died as a member of the Croatian Army 145th Brigade after being shot by Marinko M., a member of the HVO." The third paragraph reflects that Mr. Gvozden, at the time of his death, was a deputy commander of the Croatian army, 145th Brigade. And the last -- excuse me. The fourth paragraph, not the last, the fourth paragraph reflects that the claim for damages for the mother and father is 60 million Croatian dinars, and the brother and sister are claiming 40 million Croatian dinars. The next paragraph, which would be the fifth paragraph, starts with the question: "What happened near Mostar? How did Drazen Gvozden die? According to the attorney, he left for the Southern Front as a member of the Croatian Army, but at the time of his death he had HVO markings on his sleeve." This attorney, of course, is Ranko Radovic who, coincidentally, is up in the Kupreskic case representing one of the accused in that matter as we speak. The next certificate is 612, and that is a decision by the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, posthumously confirming the rank of reserve officer, the rank of reserve captain, to Drazen Gvozden. Again, this also reflects that Mr. Gvozden was part of the 145th R. Brigade from Zagreb and Dubrava. 613, Mr. President and Your Honours, is a document that is a document that comes from the Association of the Families of the Dead and the Wounded from the Republic of Croatia. This document, which is the one which has Mr. Gvozden's photograph on it, also reflects that Drazen Gvozden was a Croatian soldier in the 145th R. Brigade of the Croatian army, died on Sunday, 3 October, 1993, at the southern front. The last document is the certificate of death, and that document -- I'm sorry for the -- would be Prosecutor's Exhibit 614. This document likewise reflects that the accused was a member of the 145th Brigade and, likewise, that when he was killed, he was operating on the southern front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, we have before us clearly an HV soldier who was killed in the Mostar area on 3 October, 1993, and subsequently there was a decision charging an HVO member, Marinko Musa, with manslaughter on 9 September, 1994, and I'm, of course, talking about Prosecutor's Exhibit 609. Now, on 9 September, 1994, General, you were the chief of staff of the HVO in Mostar. As the chief of staff, did you examine this particular case and other cases of its nature where HV, or soldiers of the Republic of Croatia, were killed and wounded while operating around Mostar?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, the event took place on the 3rd of October, 1993. I am not a legal person, a lawyer. There are a lot of documents there, and I can only give my comments. On the 3rd of October, 1993, I was in the Lasva pocket confronted with the struggle for biological survival and with 35.000 refugees in the Lasva pocket. Furthermore, as the chief of the main staff linked to the 9th of September, which is when the military court prosecuted this case, I was not -- it was not my competence to supervise the work of the military court nor was I ever previously informed of this event. Everything that I learnt about it I have learnt precisely from these documents because the military court was under the inherence of the Ministry of Justice and the administration of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the Defence Ministry of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. As to the concrete events and this particular event, I have knowledge only on the basis of what I have just read from these documents and I am learning of the event here for the first time. I can state, though, that there were instances where officers and soldiers -- and that is something that the Tribunal is well aware of -- after the ceasefire was reached, interrupted their active service and took up service in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, those of them who had been born in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the most part, and they came under the personnel department of the Defence Ministry of the HVO, and I have just learnt of this case now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, the decision by the military district court or the military court was on the 9th of September, and the newspaper article that we see on the 611 is an article that was printed on the 28th of October of 1994. Now, is it your testimony that after this decision and after the filing of suit against the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, you had no knowledge of the case involving Drazen Gvozden and his death as a soldier of the Republic of Croatia while operating on the southern front?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I claim that officially I was not informed of the event and that I don't recall it. As to the 3rd of October, '93, when the event took place, I was the commander in the Lasva pocket, as I say, under complete encirclement, and that is that area there, and supervision over the military court I never had nor was I authorised as the chief of the main staff to do so. I had no -- no connection with the military court at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the witness has answered your question twice. Either on the 3rd of October he was in the Central Bosnia pocket and it was not under his jurisdiction and he's given that answer twice, so can we please try to move forward a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last question: This individual was born in Zagreb, according to his death certificate, and you just noted, General, that you had no official information. While you were the chief of staff or the deputy chief of staff or at any time prior to today, did you hear about this case involving Drazen Gvozden?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard about it today. I can't tell you whether I heard about it earlier or not, previously or not. I don't know. I try to answer to the best of my ability with respect to the documents shown me and the case in point, and I repeat that I did not have any jurisdiction, and this judgement by the military court was not sent to me. Perhaps somebody in some sort of correspondence might have asked for documents relating to this soldier, that is quite possible, but I personally have no direct knowledge about the event, and I repeat, it was a situation where I did not know how long I would survive in Vitez, and I focused my attention on survival. I was confronted with the problem of 35.000 refugees in this pocket in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But, of course, the documents that you're reading, both the judgement of the Mostar military court and the newspaper articles, were items that were published while you were in Mostar and while you were the chief of staff; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not in Mostar. I was not the chief of the main staff in Mostar. Let us be precise on that point. The headquarters of the main staff, when I was the chief of the main staff, was in Posusje, and on the 28th of October, 1994, was the time prior to the operation for the liberation of Kupres and the entire Kupres plateau, which means about 600.000 square kilometres, it was an enormous operation, and I was one of those who prepared the operation together with the commander of the 7th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course, and I mentioned that I focused my attention for the most part on combat operations there because I was the commander in a war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All this has been said before. Please. Can we try to move forward and show a little more efficiency here? The witness has answered your question. You may be happy with that, you may be unhappy with that. That's your problem. We are not going to go over what has been said over and over again. The witness has given his answer. Please, Mr. Kehoe, can you go on to another subject, or if you want to remain on that particular subject, please ask another question, a different question. Let's not go over this again and again. We'll never get it over with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That was the last question, and I am going to shift subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, we're going to shift subjects to a subject concerning the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina when you came there in April of 1992, and the first document I would like to show you, with Mr. Usher, is Prosecutor's Exhibit 406/2. Now, General, let us -- you have seen this document before. Let us direct our attention just briefly to the paragraph -- before we talk about the document, this is a document that is dated 12 November, 1991, and the names at the end are of president of the Regional Crisis Centre for Herzegovina, Mate Boban, and the president of the Travnik Regional Community, Dario Kordic. Let us look at paragraph 1 of this document dated 12 November, 1991, which reads that -- if we can just push it up just a little bit, Mr. Usher? We are going to read that paragraph going over to the next page: "The Croatian Regional Community and the Travnik Regional Community remain of the opinion stated in the conclusions adopted at earlier meetings, that the Croatian people of this region, and all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, still support the unanimously accepted orientation and conclusions adopted in agreements with president Dr. Franjo Tudjman on 13 and 20 June 1991 in Zagreb. On the basis of the conclusions of the above-mentioned meetings and agreement in Zagreb, as well as the separate conclusions of 15 October 1991 in Grude and of 22 October 1991 in Busovaca, and on this occasion, 12 November 1991, these two regional communities have unanimously decided that the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina must finally embrace a determined and active policy which will realise our eternal dream - a common Croatian State." Now, General, that issue of "an eternal dream - a common Croatian State" meant unifying Croatian sections of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the Republic of Croatia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the time when this document was compiled, the 12th of November, '91, I was in Austria, and apart from what I'm reading here in the document, these events were not previously known to me. I did not participate at any of these meetings, nor did I discuss the document with the person taking down the minutes and the president of the regional crisis committee for Herzegovina and the Travnik community with regard to this document. I do know that the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina, by way of referendum, opted for Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina based on legality. I can see what the document says. What emanates from the document, I do not have any direct knowledge. Does it mean -- may I just take another look at the document, please, read through it and have an overview of the complete document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could we try to refocus the debate, please? The problem is not for you, General, to read this document over. The witness was not present on November 12, 1991. The one thing we want to know is whether the witness shared this view of a Croatian government. Let's try to refocus the debate. The statement is quite clear. Was he in favour of this eternal state of Croatia? What is the witness's opinion about this? Was he a proponent of that particular idea? Was he against it? That's the idea we want to have a clear opinion about.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I may answer, Mr. President. In point 2 of this same document, it states that even in the leadership of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina there was still forces and so on and so forth. I don't want to read the document. I accepted to come to Bosnia-Herzegovina and give my professional assistance in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the aggression, and that was my personal position from the very start. I never took part in the elaboration of any kind of political platform, nor did I implement a political platform, including this particular political platform. I can speak of army positions, trenches and fronts where I took part as a soldier in the defence of that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's exactly what I wanted to hear. That's what we want to hear in that kind of particular debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, these two individuals that executed this document, Mate Boban was the President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and Dario Kordic was the Vice-President who was in the Central Bosnian area when you were the commander of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but at the first meeting that I attended with Mate Boban, I was told that he demanded literally that the officers of the HVO, that is to say, that the HVO be apolitical and that all political activity be left to the elected representatives of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the decree on the armed forces of the HVO also envisaged a depoliticisation of the HVO. At meetings with my associates and collaborators, I always stressed that politics was not to be our preoccupation, that is to say, the preoccupation of our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, staying with this document, in the next paragraph, if you could read this particular document, there is discussion about the Croatian Banovina. "In order that that historic goal soon may soon be our reality, these two regional communities ask that legal and political documents be prepared and published proclaiming a Croatian Banovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the holding of a referendum on joining the Republic of Croatia as the first steps on the road to the final Croatian question and the creation of..." and then the words are illegible. The next sentence in paragraph 2: "There are still forces in a segment of the HDZ/BH leadership which oppose the historic interest of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These forces are in favour of non-existent sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina in which the Croatian people would be condemned to genocide and would disappear from history." Now first, General, you have made comments before in your documents about historic interests and historic responsibility. What is this essence of historic interest or historic responsibility of the Croatian people? What does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As a soldier, within the framework of preparations to raise the combat morale of our soldiers, I would stress that in the sense that you must be up to your historical responsibilities, thinking that the history would re-examine the role of each and every soldier and each and every commander in relation to every order they received and the method and quality of the performance of their tasks. That is how I understood these historical responsibilities in the sense of raising morale. That is, anyway, the doctrinairy approach to the issuance of orders. That was one of the ways in which we were trained in the former army, and I think that this applies to any army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, the importance of this Banovina continued to be of importance and of discussion among the leaders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna even after you got to Central Bosnia on the 14th of April, 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It says in this document that documents would be published, that there would be a referendum. I have no knowledge of that referendum taking place. It may have taken place. I don't know. As I said, I participated in only two meetings of political representatives in Central Bosnia, because after I was appointed commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, I spent most of the time on the front in Jajce. That is in August, September, and much of October. I also know that at the referendum, the Croatian people opted for an independent and sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina with three constituent peoples. When you say is written in this document, but I do not know whether there was a referendum on annexation to the Republic of Croatia. As far as I recall, there was no such referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, were the discussions concerning the Banovina, did it continue after you got to Central Bosnia on the 14th of April of 1992, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you're asking me about the military aspect and the people with whom I collaborated, that is, the military commanders, I have no knowledge about that. Whether such discussions continued or not, I do not consider myself competent to answer that question because I don't know. Perhaps they did, perhaps they didn't. It is the political representatives who are better informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us talk about a couple of documents, and if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Wait. Wait a moment. This document -- General Blaskic, I'm interested in the end of this document. You have it. "In order to implement the conclusions specified in the first two points" -- can you see that? "In order to implement those aims, we must," and I'm drawing your attention to point (c) and (d), "prepare ourselves better militarily for the struggle against all forces which will attempt to stop this inevitable process of the creation of a free Croatian state," underlined, and (d), "anticipate, participate and categorically prevent any public or secret activity in the leadership which would oppose these decisions in any way." My question is the following: You're not there, you were still in Austria, but when you were appointed to assume high-level military responsibilities, did Mate Boban or Dario Kordic brief you on this project of a free Croatian state, or did they tell you, "You're just a military man and your concern is the troops exclusively"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I assume you're referring to my appointment as the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In a month's time I was the fifth commander appointed to that position, and at the time I was appointed and later on, no one asked me to implement a political platform. The situation was such that we had to focus on defence. This was a time when almost 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina was occupied by the army of Republika Srpska, in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, you told us that you were the fifth commander but, obviously, the political leaders wanted to choose somebody who would be in harmony with their political goals. Could you see Dario Kordic or Mate Boban choose somebody for such a high political post who would be contrary to their goals?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was never confronted with those political goals. I was told explicitly that the military component was depoliticised and that my assignment was a professional military assignment to prepare the defence and organise the army, the armed people. That is my understanding of it. The decree on the armed forces also stipulates that the HVO is depoliticised. I never took part in the creation of a political platform, nor was I a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You don't have to answer this question if you don't want to, but as time passed, were you in favour for a free Croatian state or for a sovereign state, that is, the sovereign state of Bosnia? If you consider this question to be prejudicial to you, you don't have to answer it, but nevertheless, one might ask one's self, who were these political leaders who had a great dream of a Croatian state and who suddenly choose a military man who would say to them, "I'm quite apolitical, and I will tell you straightaway I am in favour of the sovereignty of Sarajevo. It is something that I prefer"? Because when we see the end of this document, something doesn't seem to fit there. Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, I had a similar question sometime in March 1993, I think, at a public press conference. I spoke about those press conferences that we held in Busovaca, and I said that the HVO was struggling for our homeland, that is, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that the aim of the HVO was defence from aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is also our homeland as well, implying the equality of peoples together with the other peoples. That is what I said in March 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. You are in favour of equality. I understand that. But my last question: In this standpoint did you say to Dario Kordic or Mate Boban, at one point, "Because I am a brilliant officer, I know how to make trenches, I know how to position machine-guns, to deploy troops, but your greater Croatian state does not interest me"? Did you say that to Mate Boban or Dario Kordic at any time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had very few meetings with Mr. Mate Boban, and I became familiar with this document here in Court. So I didn't participate in its preparation, nor could I discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Don't give me that answer. I know that you were in Austria. What I'm interested in is whether you had a certain degree of political conviction when engaging or placing your military knowledge at the disposal of these inflamed politicians? Did you know what you were doing? You were struggling for a future Croatian state or were you struggling for an institutional state based in Sarajevo? What was the aim of your struggle? You came from Austria. You accepted a very risky command, General. You couldn't have been fighting for nothing.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, the government in Sarajevo ceased to function and the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina had actually collapsed. I was fighting for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina from aggression, for the establishment of a joint command. I struggled for the defence of Maglaj and Goradze, towns which had a majority Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are not answering my question. I will not insist upon it. Let me ask if my colleagues have any additional questions for you. Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I wonder if you'll help me to understand a little more clearly your statements to the effect that the army itself was not politicised. I believe you referred to the decree establishing the army and laying down its framework, and your position is that the army itself was purely professional. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is correct. My position was that we should create a professional army, that we needed to build it, develop it. It was the armed people. But they should be trained to carry out defensive military assignments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well now, the President, I think, put to you a question to this effect: He said that you were not fighting for nothing. Presumably you were fighting for something. Do you remember the president putting questions like that to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I want to ask your help on this point of clarification. Do you recognise this situation, that an army may itself be depoliticised in the sense that those who operate the army from within, like yourself, are not politicised people, that politics do not run through the functioning of the machinery of the army, but that the army is there, nevertheless, to pursue goals and to accomplish tasks set by the political directorate. So if the political directorate were, for example, to set a task of ethnic cleansing, that depoliticised army would, nevertheless, implement that political objective. Do you recognise that situation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there are several questions here. I have noted four or five. I do recognise the situation you have described, but every good soldier should also be a reasonable soldier, and he should be able to recognise such orders. The decree on the armed forces envisaged, and I am referring to it and that was also my position, because as from 1989 I ceased to be a member of the Communist Party or, rather, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and even until then I was a member on assignment. I think that the majority of the younger military men of the JNA were happy when they learned of the possibility that they had to be depoliticised and to focus on their profession. I came to Bosnia-Herzegovina and I did fight for something, and that was to help in the defence against the Serb aggression and to organise the armed people, and my idea applied to Central Bosnia. My command posts were mostly on the front lines, from the front in Sarajevo to Jajce, Maglaj, assistance to Olovo, Gorazde, and where the situation was most critical, so I fought for defence against aggression. Due to various circumstances, and there are many, a conflict occurred between two components of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the BH army and the HVO, and your question regarding the political directorate imposing certain tasks, including ethnic cleansing, I never was in a position to accept such a task of ethnic cleansing because I would not have accepted it because an obedient soldier must also be a reasonable soldier to be a good one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, I did put that branch of my question -- I don't know whether it was the fourth or fifth question -- hypothetically, but let us pursue the hypothesis a little further in order to achieve greater clarity of thought. Suppose the political directorate, it set, as one of its goals, the realisation of a Greater Croatia. Would the army under your command have worked for the achievement of that purpose?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time that I can talk about, we were not in such a position, and I believe it would not have worked in that direction because then I couldn't have been the commander of that army. A section may have existed which would have worked for that end. But, as I said, the tendency was to depoliticise the army entirely, but it is true, as you said in your question, that a certain degree of politics exists in every army, no matter how hard it may try to be clean and depoliticised, and that was not the project which prompted my arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina nor was I invited to realise such a project. I was asked to help in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I stressed that clearly at press conferences in '93, because Bosnia-Herzegovina is the state of the Croatian people of Bosnia as well, on an equal footing with the other two peoples that comprise Bosnia-Herzegovina and all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, I take it you realise that sometimes there could be a dynamic quality in the setting of purposes. You could have original purposes which change subtly or abruptly in the course of subsequent events. Should I understand you to be saying this, that if at any time the political directorate set as one of its goals the realisation of a Greater Croatia, that you would not have accepted any instructions to work for the accomplishment of that purpose?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I may just say in connection with the dynamics of goals, I may have misunderstood that process because I didn't have sufficient experience in that field and I still don't have enough experience. I don't consider myself competent to enter lengthy discussions on political issues. But I do believe that such a dynamic process exists, and this can be seen from the negotiations conducted in Central Bosnia under the auspices of the International Community. But, Your Honour, my understanding was that the task of the political representatives of the Croatian people, of the Bosniak Muslims, and the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was to participate in that dynamic process and to come to an agreement under the auspices of the International Community, to come to an agreement on the future set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I saw my role as the role of a soldier, a commander defending Bosnia-Herzegovina from aggression; and when I say "we," I mean the BH army and the HVO, had a common enemy, and that is the army of Republika Srpska which controlled a greater part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I never really studied more closely what the politicians were doing because that was their job. No one ever asked me to participate in the realisation of such a platform. At some meeting, this may have been discussed, but I was not present at those meetings, and I have no immediate knowledge that there was a discussion about the creation and the implementation of such political projects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, would it be convenient for you to summarise what would have been your reaction to a possible request by the political directorate for you to work for the realisation of a Greater Croatia? Would you have accepted those instructions or would you have declined those instructions if they were made to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No such requests were addressed to me, and I never took part in the drafting of such a platform, I personally, and I would not have implemented such a platform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Your answer --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina. We are talking about the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That sentence towards the end, that you would never have accepted such instructions, is clear, and I thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I also have a few questions for you. I am going to ask you some direct questions as far as that is possible. In your opinion, what was the best situation, from the executive point of view, if you're thinking of any organisation, from the executive point of view, what would be the best situation to say to someone who needs to do something, "In order to obtain such and such a thing, you are going to do such and such," or only to say, "You're going to do so and so"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Clearly it is best to speak frankly and to try and explain, that is, to explain the tasks and the aim of those tasks. In my view, that is a far more correct approach; that is, to provide as much information as possible, including the purpose why a particular task is being carried out, what is the purpose of such a task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: My second question is the following: To what extent can it help a soldier to know well the reasons that he is fighting for?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This can be of a great deal of assistance and it is desirable to tell the soldier the reasons behind the struggle and the aims of that struggle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the ideas that we have already discussed here, both strategic and tactical, for an officer -- I'm not talking about a soldier but an officer -- for an officer, is it important for him to know something about strategy, that is, the objectives of the tactics applied?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For an officer, it is important and it is to be expected that he would do his best to learn about the objectives of tactics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So could it be said that at a learned level of command, it is necessary to have a certain link between strategy and tactics?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At a certain level, that is necessary. These are, in most cases, the strategic operative commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You have told us that you came from Austria to Kiseljak originally for two months. What was your dream at the time? Why did you come?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I came to assist in organising and preparing the Kiseljak municipality for defence. My parents live there, the parents of my wife, my relatives. I came after invitations addressed to me by the official bodies of Kiseljak municipality, including that of my late father, my late uncle, and other of my relatives, and my intention at the time was to organise the defence and to organise the armed people in the territory of Kiseljak to defend themselves from the JNA and the Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We already know that, General, but could you tell us that you were there within the scope of a tactical plan?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And what was the strategy?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the level of Kiseljak municipality, the strategy was to survive and to prepare for the impending attack of which there was every indication because the nearby municipality of Rakovica had been cleansed and Bosnian Muslims had already come to Kiseljak at the end of April, beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General, I am asking you the same question. When you were appointed commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, what was the strategy?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The strategy, in a nutshell, because I want to be as brief as possible, was to link up all forces, all potentials of Central Bosnia for defence from Serb conquest, to try and slow down that conquest and to try to halt it. My understanding of the military situation in Central Bosnia I conveyed to the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban, and he agreed with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General, could we say that the strategy was to have an independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The strategy on the political side, as far as I know, was to establish, to achieve a political agreement on the establishment of Bosnia-Herzegovina together with representatives of the Bosniak Muslims and the Serbs with the mediation of the International Community. My military strategy was to defend as much of the remaining territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, maybe some 40 per cent, which the Serbs had still not occupied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Another question, and that will be my last. I apologise. As you know, I joined the proceedings a little later. What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am a Croat by nationality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a further point before the break. General Blaskic, could we agree on the fact that Mate Boban and Dario Kordic had a political project of a Greater Croatia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What project or programme or platform they had, I cannot say because I only had two meetings with Mr. Mate Boban. I know that he participated in the negotiations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Come on, General. I'm asking you, do you think that Mate Boban and Dario Kordic, who were the political leaders, did they have the project of creating a Croatian state and a Croatian community?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The project of a Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna within the framework of Bosnia-Herzegovina was something that they did have, and that was something that I shared, but not at the expense of Bosnia-Herzegovina but, rather, in the sense of obtaining equality of rights for Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the other peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I know that you are a military man concerned with only military things, but you just told Judge Rodrigues that as of a certain level, one does not wear black glasses and have ears plugged up. So I am saying: Among the political leaders of the Croats of Bosnia, was there a political project either of a Greater Croatia or a structured Croatian community, entity? Did this exist on the side of Mate Boban and Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, in document 406/2, from points 1 and 2, one can see that there is no unity of approach even among the HDZ leadership regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know that the Croats participated in the referendum on an independent and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the question put to me by Judge Shahabuddeen -- perhaps, at some point in time, there were such political goals, but the politics evolved and the Washington Agreement showed, one that was accepted by the Croats and I participated in the establishment of the federation army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. Let me rephrase it. In your eyes -- I am not talking about this document; you were in Austria -- in your view, did Mate Boban and Dario Kordic have a political project, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe they did have a political programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What was that political project, in your view?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my view, that political project was to ensure equality of rights of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the mediation of the International Community and through an agreement with the other constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: According to what you know, is that what they tried to realise or did they try to achieve something else, in fact, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the basis of what I know, and my only sources are the negotiations that were carried out with the mediation of the International Community, as far as I know, the Croatian side was cooperative in those negotiations with the mediation of the International Community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. I am asking you whether Mate Boban and Dario Kordic had a political project, and if they did, did they try to implement it through this Croatian community of defence?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If they had a project, I am again conveying my opinion, it is possible that they tried to implement that programme through their activities, but I am speaking on the basis of the knowledge I have about the international negotiations conducted through the mediation of the International Community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. But beyond that information, General Blaskic, you were the operative commander of Central Bosnia. After all, you were not blind regarding the newspapers, deaf regarding the radio and television, so you cannot just say "I was a simple soldier." You were not a simple soldier. My question is: At a given point in time, after the spirit of two months, when you focused on the defence of Kiseljak, did you say at a certain point to yourself that you had been manipulated by Mr. Mate Boban and Mr. Dario Kordic, that they were pursuing a political goal whereas you were simply intent on defending your Bosnian Croatian territory against the Serbs? Did you have a feeling that you had been manipulated by them?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, allow me to say that in the territory where I was, the territory was isolated, there was no electricity or water, there was no press. I didn't have occasion to read the daily newspapers. It was a very difficult situation we were in. I had 35.000 refugees in that area. But it is a fact that there was an about-turn within the Croatian leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina politically because Mr. Boban handed in his resignation and Kresimir Zubak took over to implement the federation. The circumstances under which he handed in his resignation I don't know because I wasn't there. I have no immediate knowledge. But probably a certain about-turn did take place and new people were chosen to implement the Washington Agreement. I'm talking about the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Rodrigues? Then we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Just to round off this part of the discussion, there is something I would like to understand. Your project of your life was to abandon a military career. You asked to leave the JNA. You had a concept of life or a dream in Austria of life in Austria with your wife and so on. You accepted to come to Kiseljak for two months to organise the defence. I understand that because there were certain emotional reasons, but without soldiers, without structures, without any proper organisation, et cetera, et cetera, you decided to stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that there must have been some very strong reasons. Your idea was not, after all, to become a general. Your military career was something that you had abandoned. In view of all these circumstances - how can I put it - adverse circumstances, you stayed, nonetheless, and, therefore, I think there were some very strong reasons, and I should really like to understand what were those reasons if you abandoned your entire military career.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, you said yourself that there were reasons, emotional and others, for my coming. There was a war which brought with it many unforeseeable circumstances, including the fact that I stayed on. This territory of Central Bosnia that we managed to defend cost me, as a commander, I'm sorry to have to say that, it cost me more than 2.000 graves, more than 5.000 wounded, and 22 members of my family including my father, that is, my broader family. Twenty-two members were lost in all. I stayed after the signing of the Washington Agreement, believing that we would be able to develop the army of the federation. I took part in the final operations, together with the BH army, despite this one-year long tragic war. My plans were not linked to a career in the army, because I also studied civilian subjects, hoping to abandon my military career. I believed I would be able to do that after the implementation of the Washington and possibly the Dayton agreements. But I also spoke to Mr. Kresimir Zubak, as the President of the federation, and he expressed the wish that I should continue first as deputy chief of staff and then chief of staff in the HVO, focusing on professionals and people from Bosnia-Herzegovina to build this army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that we are going to have a break. The interpreters have worked hard, so the break will last until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, just a few questions based on some of your responses to the Trial Chamber. You noted, in response to both a question from the President and also from Judge Rodrigues, in referring to paragraph 3(c), which notes that they must make better military preparations for combat against those forces which will attempt to stop this inevitable process of creation of a free Croatian state, now, you noted in response, and I believe this is specifically to a question by Judge Rodrigues, that your strategy, in a nutshell, was to link up all potential forces for the defence against Serb consequence and halt it. Do you recall saying that to Judge Rodrigues?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it was a question, Your Honours, of the time I was in Kiseljak as the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. I think that that was so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you, General, Prosecutor's Exhibit 502. Yet, General, within a month of you coming to Kiseljak, you issue an order, Prosecutor's Exhibit 502, which is an order that came from Mate Boban, down to General Roso, that you issued, declaring the Territorial Defence illegal. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what is stated in point 5, but the document is dated the 11th of May, 1992, when the Territorial Defence of the JNA made up the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And when the Yugoslav People's Army was still the legal armed force which was there to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, that particular order is dated the 11th of May, 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the 11th of May, 1992 the JNA was present in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is the same day that you noted, to an Agence France Presse reporter, that with regard to the embattled Bosnia-Herzegovina government in Sarajevo, you say, "It has no legitimacy here." The same day, while you say that you are trying to galvanise the forces for a fight against the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Compound. One question at a time, Your Honour, particularly given the translation. The question is compound. Mr. Kehoe asked several questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I well understand what you mean, Mr. Kehoe, but I also well understand the nature of Mr. Hayman's objection. You are putting several questions to the witness at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. I apologise. I will break the questions down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The day, the same day that you order that the Territorial Defence forces are rendered invalid, an article is published in the Agence France Presse where you is say that the government in Sarajevo has no legitimacy here, and "here" means Kiseljak. The same day.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would like to see what the question was asked me linked to that legitimacy, but I will clarify the circumstances we found ourselves in. Kiseljak was the border area bordering on the area controlled by the Serbs. The JNA, together with the army of the Republika Srpska and the government in Sarajevo, and in concrete terms, I have in mind the Defence Ministry, by a fax line, sent its orders demanding that the city of Sarajevo be deblocked. Sarajevo is about 30 kilometres away from Kiseljak, as far as I know. So orders of this kind, as they arrived into the hands of the army of the Republika Srpska, could have caused direct action by the artillery, and that whole area could have been burned at a time when there were several hundred armed soldiers or people in Kiseljak. On many occasions, I cautioned them about this and asked that they should not react to Kiseljak in that way because, quite obviously, some institutions wanted to involve Kiseljak into a war without any reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, please, try to help the Judges by answering directly the question that has been directly put to you. You're not helping at all by answering it that way. A moment ago you told Judge Rodrigues and Judge Shahabuddeen that you are not a political man, that you did not have political opinion, and here we have a declaration which seems to contradict the order that was emitted on that very same day. So that's a problem. Please try to help us. The question was clear, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you understand the question, General?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, he asked to see the Agence France Presse report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's not in Serbo-Croat. He's being asked to interpret a public statement and he should get to see it. That would be our request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Hayman. You're quite right. But I think that Mr. Kehoe was thinking that the General could remember this interview. But, indeed, I think it would be best for the witness to have the text of this interview before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would note, Mr. President, for the record, that when this witness, when this particular article was addressed to him during his last week of cross-examination, admitted that he made these statements. We can go back in the transcript and find that particular provision. It will take me over the lunch-hour to do that but I will find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. Kehoe. Like you, I think we are losing a lot of time, but we are talking here of a fundamental right of the witness, of any witness, and here the witness is the accused, so he does have the right to read a document when we're asking him to compare two documents. But let's try to do this as efficiently and quickly as possible. Would it be possible to find that document easily, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is. I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar. It is Prosecutor's Exhibit 545, 545.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. The original document is French, as we are talking here of the Agence France Presse, French press agency. Do you have this in the English version?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, we have this in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think what you can do, Mr. Kehoe, is read the relevant paragraph and the translators will work and help the witness understand what you're saying. So can you please read the relevant part of this text, Mr. Kehoe, the part you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Excuse me, Mr. Usher, can we just go up there a little bit more? That paragraph, and I believe, Mr. President, it's 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, where Blaskic is named. It begins: "Tiho Blaskic, who heads the CVO forces in Kiseljak, explained that the region was peaceful because the Serbs, who make up only three per cent of the town's population 'have no designs on this land.' "As for the embattled Bosnia-Herzegovina government in Sarajevo, 'It has no legitimacy here,' he said." If we turn to the next page, Mr. Usher, and we look at the last two paragraphs on page 2, it reads as follows: "Kiseljak would henceforth be a part of a Croatian canton and administrative region and would look to the west rather than the east, Tiho Blaskic said. "'Its closeness to Sarajevo never contributed much to our town anyway,' he said." Now, General, you've had an opportunity to hear the translation of this article that you previously told us that you said, this article is published on the same day where you issue an order outlawing the Territorial Defence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The date of the order is identical to the interview, but allow me to clarify matters. The order was issued on the basis of receiving an order from the main staff, and as I already said, at that time military conscripts from Kiseljak had -- and I know this in concrete terms because my late father was to report to Breza or Ilijas -- and they could have been called up by that same JNA or the Territorial Defence for mobilisation in Ilijas in an area already under the control of Serbia, that is to say, the army of Republic of Serbia or the JNA. As far as the Serbs in Kiseljak are concerned and the 3 per cent mentioned, I have in mind the municipality of Kiseljak and the villages which gravitate towards Ilidza, and of those Serbs, the danger did not come from those Serbs and they were never attacked by the HVO. In a later period, they were, by the Territorial Defence. Now, how the translation was that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had no legitimacy, perhaps because it was not linked to the area, but this Tribunal knows that I personally sent written reports to the Defence Minister in Sarajevo in August 1992 when he asked me to do so, and I received orders, it is a whole series, a set of orders, from the Supreme Command staff of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the deblocking of Sarajevo and participation in that deblocking operation and I informed my superiors of that. As far as where Kiseljak would be, I don't know in what context the question was raised, but I could refer back to negotiations, if they were held, the negotiations that were held through the mediation of international representatives. I said that we were interested in the West and not the East. I said that previously, and I think that in the transcript you will see my position linked to that commentary in the sense that it was the aspiration of everybody from the region, that is how I understood it, Western democracy and not what is happening in the East, having in mind the JNA and all those that the people had to defend themselves against.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, your comment that the government in Sarajevo "has no legitimacy here," keep that in mind because I would like to ask you to compare that to a quote that Mate Boban gave to a reporter, Ed Vulliamy, on the 13th of August of 1992, and that, Mr. President and Your Honours, is on page 7754 on line 15, where Boban told Mr. Vulliamy -- and, Judge Rodrigues, Mr. Vulliamy was a reporter for The Guardian who testified previously, as I'm sure you know. Boban told Vulliamy he could not accept the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its capital, Sarajevo. Now, that quote to Mr. Vulliamy is remarkably similar to your quote where you say that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo "has no legitimacy (in Kiseljak)"; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already commented and said that I didn't have the interview in my hands previously and that I had in mind that -- I meant that it had no influence, and how that complete translation was made, that it absolutely has no legitimacy, Franjo Boras and Jerko Doko asked me for a report, and if I sent the report to the Defence Minister, I don't know in what context the translation of what I said was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, that is not the real problem here. First of all, I would tell Mr. Kehoe that the question is not to ask, "What do you think about a statement made by Mate Boban?" the question here is not about the word "legitimacy," maybe that's not really what you wanted to say at the time, but we are interested by the whole of this interview. The whole of this statement is quite political in its nature. My question is the following: A moment ago you told us that you were a general, a military man who was not involved in politics, and here in this particular document we find at least three sentences where it appears that you do take an interest in politics, that as a general you are a little interested in politics. It is not something, you know, I am criticising, but I see there that you are a general who is a little bit interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, quite possibly in the question there are some political elements, but at that time I was a Captain First Class of the former Yugoslav People's Army who had arrived 15 days previously, or some 20 days prior to this, to Kiseljak after spending several years -- after spending years away from the area, and I don't know what context the questions were asked in, I can't remember the context and why the answers were as they were, but my preoccupations were always the army and military issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yet, General, within four months of this particular interview, you are at a meeting with other members of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and you are preparing and receive instructions to prepare for combat operations against the Muslims, four months later, in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That question is not exact because you are suggesting an answer. I was not preparing for combat operations against the Muslims in September of 1992. I had come to the meeting having been invited to attend for them to get to know me, to introduce me to the other political and other representatives who were present at the meeting, and the overall circumstances were such that at that time the most fierce operations were being fought, Jajce, Maglaj, Olovo, Travnik, and so on and so forth, and from numerous documents you can see that we tried to pool our efforts there, the BH army and the HVO, in a joint defence, particularly for Travnik and Maglaj, Usora, Olovo and other regions, and at that particular meeting, I did not receive any assignments nor could I have received any, and the chief of the main staff was the only one to be able to give me orders, and from the political representatives in Central Bosnia, I received no orders for any assignments or tasks whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, I ask you to take a look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/95, and I ask you to go to the last page of that document, when you receive it, and focus on the second-to-last paragraph of that document. Second-to-last paragraph, last page, Mr. Usher. That paragraph -- and this is an excerpt from the minutes of the meeting of the Croatian Defence Council in municipalities of Central Bosnia dated 22 September, 1992, where you, General, are one of the members of the working presidency along with Dario Kordic, Anto Valenta, and Ignac Kostroman. This paragraph reads that: "HVO Military bodies for Central Bosnia shall prepare defence plans against possible attack by Islamic Fundamentalist Mujahedin Forces and introduce military discipline and order in the military formations."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the translation is completely wrong. It is an absolutely erroneous translation of the text. The English text that we have here, there are two paragraphs which have been merged into one, and the sense of what is written in the original Croatian text has been lost, and I propose that the Croatian translation, that the Croatian original, that is to say, be placed on the ELMO, and that the interpreters who are here now should interpret it, and you will see that the English translation is wrong, it is substantially different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I quite agree with you, Mr. Nobilo, it does seem necessary, so we will put the Croatian version on the ELMO, please. Which is the paragraph you are quarrelling with?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is the last page, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have this in its French version, but I will try to find my way around. Last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Last page, second-to-last paragraph. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How do you want to go about this, Mr. Nobilo? The Judges have now before them the B/C/S version. I have a French version of the text. I am going to hand it over to my two colleagues. But I would like to have the interpreters help us understand this clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I suggest that I read out the text in Croatian and then the interpreters will translate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I suggest that the interpreters just read it in the translation as they translate it, with the proper inflections the way the translators view it, with all due respect to counsel, so the translators could read it in and of themselves. This, I would note, is a translation that came from the translation department. Of course, neither Mr. Harmon nor I speak B/C/S, so this is a translation received from the ICTY. Nevertheless, if the translators can translate that, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but this particular paragraph is said by Mr. Nobilo to be incorrect, so I would like Mr. Nobilo or a Serbo-Croatian interpreter to read this paragraph and then the other interpreters will work into their respective language and everything will be much simpler that way. How do you want to go about this exactly? Mr. Nobilo, do you want to read this? I think that is the best solution. Just go ahead and read this paragraph, the first paragraph, to begin with. Read slowly, please. It starts with "Vojni organi."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is important because it is important for it to enter into the transcript, the text itself, because if it appears that the text is different, as I consider, then it will have to be changed, the translation of the document of the Prosecution will have to be changed. So I am going to start reading slowly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute, Mr. Nobilo. What's important right now is for you to read this text aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore, I am reading the text as follows: "Military organs of the HVO of Central Bosnia are duty-bound to elaborate plans of defence from a possible attack by the Islamic Fundamentalist Mujahedin Forces which have been infiltrated into the organs of the army of BH as well." And then the second paragraph ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you please repeat -- wait. It's very different indeed. Mr. Nobilo, I'm sorry, but indeed the French version I have before me says that "The military organs will introduce disciplinary measures in the military formations," which is quite different from what you have just said. So please repeat what you've just said. Can the interpreters help us once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The question is of "Islamic Fundamental Mujahedin Forces which have been infiltrated also into the organs of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is so far from what I have before me that I'm unable to say anything. Let's go to the next paragraph. In my translation, it seems that "the Ministry of Defence will ensure military logistics for Central Bosnia in conjunction with the military command." That's not at all what you've just been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm going to read the next passage: "Military organs of Central Bosnia are duty-bound to speed up, accelerate, the procedure of the professionalisation of military units and to establish full military discipline and order into military units."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Right. We can find some elements which are common to what you've just said and my translation, but clearly there is a problem. Mr. Registrar, is this an official translation emanating from the CLSS? I'm talking about the French translation here because I can only judge what is said in the French document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just a second, please. I have to check something. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, with the agreement of the two other Judges, we will ask you, Mr. Nobilo, to read this paragraph again slowly, the interpreters will give us their translation of the document, and this will be entered in the minutes of the hearing, and then I will ask the CLSS section, via the registry, to give us a new translation of that paragraph. Please read again slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am reading the text: "The military organs of the HVO of Central Bosnia are duty-bound to elaborate plans of defence against a possible attack from Islamic Fundamentalist Mujahedin Forces which have infiltrated into the organs of the army of BH as well." And now a new paragraph, the next paragraph: "Military organs of Central Bosnia are duty-bound to accelerate the process of professionalisation for the military units and to establish full military discipline and order into military units." And that is the end of the quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There are two points that are very different from what we have before our eyes. One speaks of professionalisation and not about logistics and then there is what is said in the first paragraph which is one which is not clear at all. In this new translation we have just got, we speak about Mujahedin forces which have infiltrated the BiH army forces, so it's very different from what we had before us. I will ask for a new official translation. It's five past one. We are going to take a break for lunch, and we will try to gather again with a new translation. I think it is the simplest way to go about this. The witness must be able to make comments on documents that everybody agrees on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will meet again at 2.30. I am giving back the document to the registrar. The hearing is adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, as well as the counsel of the Defence and the Prosecution, please take note that tomorrow, Wednesday, we will begin at 10.00 for a normal day, as Tuesday and Thursday. However, for this week there is a change for Thursday and Friday. Thursday morning we will not be sitting, and we will resume Thursday afternoon at 3.30. On Friday morning we will sit from 10.00 rather than 9.00. Have you taken note of that, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is for reasons of security and the special units that provide transportation of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, the particular document we were talking about, 456/95, on the 22nd of September 1992, is a document which has political aspects to it; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It is a document that emanated from the regular meetings of the civilian officials of Central Bosnia, and it covers more or less all aspects, but I would like to mention that I became familiar with this document here in the courtroom. Though it says that I was a member of the working presidency, clearly all the members of the working presidency signed it but I did not. I did not receive it before coming here to the Tribunal, nor was I familiar with this document. I did know about the discussion and the contents of the discussion to the extent I was able to learn about those discussions during the meeting. I was a guest at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, you told us this morning that you only had attended two meetings with political representatives in Central Bosnia. Is that what you told the Judges this morning?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were very few meetings, possibly only two. This was a meeting of familiarisation, where I was introduced to the civilian authorities in September 1992. Another meeting of coordinating bodies like this one was held in April 1993, which I attended. However, these meetings actually took place every fortnight in Central Bosnia, but these were meetings of civilian representatives and I did not attend those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could put Prosecutor's Exhibit 572/1 on the ELMO? If we could pan back just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let's go through these individuals. The man on the left is Ignac Kostroman, the secretary of the HVO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is Ignac Kostroman. I think that he was the Secretary-General of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina. He may have been of the HVO. In any event, he was a secretary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was a political figure, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was a political figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The man next to him is Anto Valenta the Deputy President of the HVO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Anto Valenta was the Deputy Prime Minister of the government of HVO, I think, or the coordinator for Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as of the 8th of April, this was a man who actually had an office down the hall from you in the Hotel Vitez; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. That was a man who was thrown out of his office in Travnik because of the various events that took place there, and he used the office of the chief of staff, that is, Mr. Franjo Nakic for a time from April the 8th in the Vitez Hotel, but for a very brief time. Then he had an office in a nearby building. I don't know the name of the building, but it was across the street from the hotel, about a hundred metres down the road. He couldn't go back to Travnik because the BH army had occupied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Valenta was a political figure also, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Valenta was, as I have already mentioned the positions he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next to Valenta and next to you, in between you and Valenta, is Dario Kordic, the vice president of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was a political figure also?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was a political figure too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you met with these men at these press conferences at least once a week in Busovaca; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't meet with these men, I was a participant in the press conference, as can clearly be seen.
