The press conferences were held more or less weekly, and they were open to the public, attended by representatives of the United Nations and other representatives of the media, and I was amongst those answering questions addressed by journalists, but each one was responsible for his department. I was responsible for military issues. So this was not a meeting with political representatives as implied from this document that we spoke of from '92 or the other one referred to that was held in April '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, these press conferences that you attended on a weekly basis, politics involving the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was discussed by Kostroman, Valenta, and Kordic in your presence; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They answered the questions of journalists in my presence. I did not ask them any questions, nor did I participate in any kind of discussions with them at those press conferences. As I said, these were press conferences attended by members of the press from that local community, and depending on the questions, that is, whether they were political or civilian, each of the individuals answered. If there were military questions, as this was a period of heavy fighting first with the Republika Srpska and then with the BH army, I was the one who answered those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, based on those questions, General, you were well aware of the political positions of these three men, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could hear, like the other people in attendance, the positions presented by these representatives, but let me repeat that this was not a meeting with the civilian representatives. I stick by my assertion that I attended only two meetings. A meeting is one thing and a press conference is another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, at these press conferences where political platforms were being discussed or political commentary was being made by these three men, did you ever disagree with them publicly?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They made their comments. Those comments were not binding upon me. There were some I did not agree with. I did have occasion to tell some of them so, but those comments they made did not concern me. I was in charge of the command and as a soldier I received my orders from the main staff, and the statements of local or regional political representatives were not binding upon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, those political statements that you disagreed with, tell the Judges about those political statements that you disagreed with and to whom did you direct your criticisms and when?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is hard for me to say when. On one occasion, during a press conference of this kind when we were without running water and electricity, this was a period of conflict with the BH army, it may have been at the end of 1993, I remember that Mr. Valenta said that he condemned such an approach by the BH army, that is, depriving the Lasva pocket of water and electricity, and he said that if this continued the HVO would take measures to cut off the power and water wherever the HVO could do so for the members of the BH army and in the areas inhabited by Bosniak Muslims. I told him personally that I did not support that and that I would no longer attend such press conferences at which such statements would be made, and I disagreed with this statement that he made to the press at the press conference. I think that from then on he did not attend those press conferences, but instead there were separate press conferences held by him as a representative of the civilian authorities and press conferences of the command of Central Bosnia at which military issues were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, is that it? Is that the only one that you can recall that you disagreed with?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You asked me when and where. There may have been other occasions. I wish to remind Their Honours that there were quite a number of statements by political representatives, including local people. We can see from this document that the municipal level almost determined what the Ministries and the army would do. However, I considered that such statements had no binding effect upon me, and I acknowledged the superiority only of the main staff and the official orders I received from them. But there were many statements of local officials but these were not official positions or official documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, isn't it a fact, sir, that you were involved in politics, as we saw from the Agence France Presse article, through this meeting on the 22nd of September, 1992 up through your political commentary on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it is not a fact. Unfortunately, I was preoccupied with our struggle for survival. One should bear in mind that I spent the whole of August at the front in Jajce, in September again, most of the time on the front line in Jajce; October, at the front line in Travnik. I can show you where my command posts were, and I claim that the front line was my command post in Jajce and Travnik. The headquarters was based in Vitez, but I spent most of my time focusing on military issues. So these two meetings, or the one you are referring to, is not an indicator of my political participation, the more so as I was introduced at the meeting as a guest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, you made political commentary on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did comment on the Vance-Owen Plan, which was a plan on the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but specifically the part relating to military issues and the military aspects of that plan, to the extent to which I was informed about that plan, because the Vance-Owen Plan was not just a political plan, it was a plan covering the overall political set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina, going into political as well as military aspects. Perhaps I was not fully qualified for the political part, but I did comment on the military aspect of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, let us show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/112, a document you discussed with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps before going on, Judge Rodrigues has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. General Blaskic, how many times, more or less, were you seated in this way as shown on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is hard for me to say how many times, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But roughly.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sometimes it was once a week, sometimes once a fortnight; it depended on the conditions, the situation on the battlefront, what the needs were, whether we had anything to say at that press conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Another question: Why did you say that Kostroman, Kordic, and Valenta, on this photograph, are politicians, are political figures? Why?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because they had certain political positions in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, later the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and before that in the HDZ party. They were members of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, but if you look at the photograph, I think that one can see Kordic and Kostroman in military clothing.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, virtually all civilian representatives at some point in time, I can't say throughout the period of the war, but for a long time during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina wore military uniforms, including Mr. Valenta. So I am really surprised that in this photograph he is in civilian clothes. I saw him many times wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But a picture speaks more loudly than words, and if a person looks at this photograph, without seeing what those people have in their minds, in their heads, who are civilians and who are the military men?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a good question. Pictures do say a lot, and one might conclude from this picture that all are soldiers except one. However, in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, from the age of childhood, children of five and onwards, love to wear uniforms, especially camouflage uniforms. It was a piece of clothing that was most in demand in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So a normal person looking at this photograph would say there is one civilian and three military men, but in effect there were three political figures and only one military man because you said that this photograph -- or this meeting which you attended on many occasions, you knew very well that a photograph speaks more loudly than words, yet you accepted to be seated under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and these were, as I said, press conferences, and they were the only way of conveying certain positions to the population of the pocket, be they military or political or civilian. But I mostly discussed military issues at those press conferences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Imagine, General, that this is a press conference, and there may be journalists from the BBC, CNN, or foreign journalists, and they have a military question. If I understood you well, you said that you were there to answer questions of a military nature. If I am a journalist, a foreign journalist, in the hall attending a press conference, I have a military question perhaps, and I could address myself either to Kostroman or to Kordic; perhaps I will ask you that question because I may like you more. But if I have a military question, I could easily address myself to the other people, but I would never address the question to Anto Valenta, who is wearing a tie. Do you think that I would be reasonable?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, because all three are wearing uniforms. But there are two more details that could be mentioned. If a question was of a military nature, then the interpreter would address the question to me, and this badge shown here was worn for the benefit of foreign journalists and it said that I was the military commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, whereas the others did not wear such a badge, and then the questions would be addressed to the persons responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: One more question, General Blaskic. Under these conditions that we see on the photograph, who chaired the meeting? Who chaired the proceedings at this table?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No one acted as chairman. There was a kind of master of ceremonies. We can't see him, I think he was seated to my left, and he sort of conducted the proceedings. He would just say, "I am opening this press conference of Central Bosnia. Today's guests are so and so." And if I may just add, this was not a conference attended only by HVO members. For instance, on the 16th of November, 1992, sitting next to me at the same conference was the president of the war presidency of Gorazde municipality, Mr. Hadzo Efendic, who came to thank me and the command in public for assistance in the defence of Gorazde. So there were other guests, representatives of the Territorial Defence and others, who attended such conferences, but no one really acted as chairman. If a conference was convened regarding certain negotiations on the internal set-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then those questions would be answered by the political representatives. That was the only way in which we could communicate, except for the official information that reached us in those days, that could reach us under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just following up on Judge Rodrigues' question, General, in addition to these weekly meetings, how many times a week did you speak to or meet Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I repeat, these were not weekly meetings. Perhaps I didn't get the correct interpretation. Because for me, a meeting was a form of work and something quite different than weekly meetings for the public, these were conferences for the public, whereas meetings with Dario Kordic -- how many times a week? -- sometimes not at all. If necessary, we would meet if he had some information linked to my needs, that is to say, to military matters. We would meet in the church, for example, if I was in the church at Busovaca. But there was no regular form of contact because he was not my superior. My superior was the chief of the main staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, on average, in addition to these weekly press conferences, how often did you meet Kordic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that it wasn't standard, there was no standard preconceived order. Sometimes once a week, sometimes I would meet him during the mass said in the church in Busovaca and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Ignac Kostroman went to many meetings with international agencies that you attended; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that is not so. Ignac Kostroman attended meetings -- I can even try and enumerate them -- from the 23rd of October, when there was a broader delegation of the HVO at a meeting, in the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and at the military airport, and the meeting was convened by General Morillon. The next meeting was held, I think it was on the 30th of October, and the following one in November, perhaps even the 5th of November, and at the March meeting in Zenica -- there was a March meeting in Zenica. Very few meetings where he was present; in fact, I would say five, between five, five, six, or seven meetings, to the best of my recollection. Perhaps he went to meetings that I did not have any knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in addition to these press conferences, approximately how often did you meet with Kostroman?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he had a completely different department. He was the secretary, and the situation was similar as with Kordic, and far less frequently because I had my command in Vitez and I spent most of my time up at the front line, so that throughout August in Jajce, throughout October and November in Travnik, in Zepce, in Usora, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Valenta, in addition to these press conferences, how often did you meet with Valenta?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was invited by Chairman Thebault once to attend a meeting, perhaps two or three times. I saw him in the hotel when he was staying there temporarily, but any meetings with him, apart from the meetings that I was invited to attend by the international -- European Monitors, and I think it was Colonel Stewart at the time, I had no other meetings with Valenta, and I did not consider that I was duty-bound to have meetings with him, to meet him, because none of the positions of Valenta, Kostroman, or anybody were binding for me, apart from the official orders issued by the chief of the main staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, wasn't Valenta present at one of your meetings with Colonel Stewart where the issues on Ahmici were discussed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He wasn't present. The meeting was in his office, the meeting was in May 1993, and I don't know all the topics of the meeting. There was a whole delegation of European Monitors there headed by their representative, Mr. Thebault. There was also Colonel Stewart there. They invited me to attend that meeting, for a portion of that meeting which was when there was a discussion on Ahmici and the investigation in Ahmici and other subjects as well, and if you want me to, I can look at my notes and chronology and tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the appropriate time, General, we'll get back to that. At this juncture, let us turn our attention to your political commentary on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan as reflected in Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/112. Now, General, this was a document that was discussed during your direct-examination, which Mr. Nobilo described at page 20110 as a potentially troublesome document, and referring to this document, Mr. Nobilo referred to it as involving political issues. Now, this document not only quite clearly does involve political issues in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan; isn't that correct? This is a document that is dated the 26th of May, 1993 and is sent to the European Union Monitoring Mission, Mr. Thebault. Again, I ask you, this is a document that quite clearly discusses political issues, isn't that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I'd like to say something about the document. The document, judgingly the initials, was written by Drago Dujmovic, and I said -- and not only did he write it but he signed it. He did not have authorisation to do so, because he was not amongst the ranks of my assistants to able to sign a document of this kind. Had I known, this kind of document would never have been sent out from my command to Mr. Thebault. Mr. Thebault had a series of meetings with me, and I never discussed the political aspects with him and political issues with him, and he knows that full well. As far as the Vance-Owen Plan is concerned and what the Prosecutor maintains that it only treated political questions, perhaps I don't understand Vance-Owen's plan properly, but it's my position that it treated questions of state administration and the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and structure included, political questions, military issues, and a series of other questions including the setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself as the state of three constituent peoples. That is a plan which was created under the chairmanship of international intermediaries. That is how I understand it. But as I underline, I did not authorise the document and I do not stand behind the document, although the last passage, the last paragraph of the document calls for a joint meeting for us to clarify things that were not clear. I never discussed political matters with the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me be very clear about the reference to political issues, General, and I will read you Mr. Nobilo's question and then your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is, counsel, for your reference, page 20174 beginning on line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is Mr. Nobilo's questions concerning this document, Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/112. "Q So this is a letter to the monitoring mission of the European Community where your name has been typed out and references made to political issues such as the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan." The question says: "Q So tell us, did you write this? Did you sign it? Would you have signed it and sent such a document?" Your answer is, beginning on line 3 of page 201175: "A I did not approve this document. I did not write it and I did not sign it. This document was signed by Mr. Drago Dujmovic. He was the officer in the department for information and propaganda activities, and he never held such a position that would authorise him to sign any document on my behalf." Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Counsel, I believe you misquoted the transcript on line 5 when you said, "Signed by Mr. Drago Dujmovic." The transcript says, "Written by Mr. Drago Dujmovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Counsel, you're right. It does say in the transcript it was written by Mr. Drago Dujmovic. I believe the rest of it is accurate. "A He was the officer of the department of information and propaganda activities, and he never held such a position that would authorise him to sign any document on my behalf."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, is that true, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dujmovic was never in a position to sign any documents on your behalf; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Dujmovic was not in that kind of position, authorising him sign documents on my behalf. He was not an assistant. It was only my assistants who were authorised to sign those documents. As far as I know, he did not perform the function of assistant for political activities except after Marko Prskalo had been wounded. I think Dragan Ramljak then held the post of assistant for political matters in the military district of Vitez. But at all events, a document with contents of this kind I would not have sent to Mr. Thebault, nor did I discuss political matters with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, General.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 615 and 615A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this is an order of the 30th of April, 1993. Again, you would agree with me that it is drafted by Drago Dujmovic, and whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, counsel has characterised this as an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's a request for invention. I apologise, counsel. You're absolutely right. Request for intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Whose signature is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is also Drago Dujmovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you authorise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would have to read through it to see what it is about. May I please read the document to refresh my memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Generally speaking -- excuse me for interrupting, but generally speaking, I'm talking to you, General Blaskic, it is a bit confusing. When we have orders, requests, whatever the type of document, that bear your seal and are written by somebody else, you sometimes say, "No, I don't approve of this." It's a bit confusing, don't you think? Can you imagine me tomorrow morning giving a decision bearing my seal and then saying later on, "Well, no. This was written by my assistant. I don't authorise this document. I don't approve of it." This is a general question, which has nothing to do with this particular document, but it seems to me that since the beginning we have seen the documents with the seal of General Blaskic, and we hear you saying, "This was written by such and such and he had no power to write such a document." So it is a bit confusing, all the more so when we only have an English version or a French version that says "Tihomir Blaskic" at the end of a document. It's very exceptional for me to have the B/C/S/ version before me. Because the only thing we see on French and English versions is your name "Tihomir Blaskic," which is a bit confusing and a bit perplexing, don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is quite right. It is a little confusing, because according to the regulations of the work of the command of the Operative Zone, documents were to be signed by me. If I couldn't sign them, then it would be the chief of the main staff, Franjo Nakic, who would sign them. But he was absent for a number of -- for a long time because he was working on the commissions. We all know about this. I don't want to repeat it. So if I wasn't there, then my assistants could sign the documents. But Drago Dujmovic was never officially an assistant, he was a clerk. The assistant was Marko Prskalo, who had been wounded and he was lying wounded in hospital. Now, I don't know, chronologically speaking, when his deputy took up his duties for him to be able to sign, but clerks were not, as a rule, able to sign documents as my assistants and deputies, because that would mean that 500 -- well, not 500, but 50 other people could have signed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I repeat that my question is of a general nature, General Blaskic. Generally speaking, do you think that you were the man responsible for all the documents bearing the seal of Tihomir Blaskic, because you don't only put your seal on these documents, if we are speaking of a traditional organisation, there's something that's striking in these documents, because not only do we see the seal of the commander of the Operative Zone, but we also see his name, your name, typewritten on the document. Sometimes it is your signature also that appears but sometimes it is not your signature. So my question is very simple. Generally speaking, do you feel you are responsible for all the documents bearing your seal and bearing your name?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I feel myself responsible, Mr. President and Your Honours, but all documents in the command of the Operative Zone for Central Bosnia bear my name and that same stamp. All the documents. Those were our internal rules. So you have the commander, regardless of who signed the document. What I want to say is that the right to sign was something that my deputies had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, please, there are two different categories of documents. You give to your assistants the possibility to sign some documents. If you give that authorisation to your assistants, you are responsible, in a way, for what he's going to do. If you don't want to be responsible for what this assistant is going to do, you will not give him the authorisation to put a signature on the document. Either you give your signature or you don't. If you do give it, then you are responsible. Again, I'm speaking in very general terms. Let's forget about Blaskic for the moment being. So either one gives his or her signature, or one doesn't.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I have understood you correctly, but I consider myself to be responsible for the documents which bear my name and surname, and every document in the Operative Zone has my name and surname on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for this very clear answer. That's quite clear. I bring your attention to the fact that we are speaking of two categories of documents, internal documents where, of course, you might think you are responsible, but also documents who go outside the Operative Zone and who are meant for the BritBat, for example; for external organisations; for the ECMM, for example; for the Red Cross, for example. These documents -- I'm sure you must feel particularly responsible for these documents. You feel responsible for all the documents but particularly for these documents, because how do you want the Red Cross, for example, to know who is in charge of the Operative Zone if you say, "Oh, no. I'm sorry, but my assistant has done something I don't agree with." These documents are very important ones. They are, you know, sent to the Red Cross or to the ECMM. You have to agree with what I'm saying, don't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree, but on this document, once again, the date is the 30th of April, 1993, and I'm sure you know the confusion that reigned from the 100 offices necessary. Only seven of us worked. Two were wounded and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I can understand that answer you've just given me, but I was speaking in general terms. You make comments, you know, about such and such a document by saying, "Yes, I was, you know, on the front. There was a slight misunderstanding," et cetera. That I can understand. But what I want to appear in this transcript is that General Blaskic considers himself as responsible for every document going outside the Operative Zone, documents which bear his signature and his name, Tihomir Blaskic. Thank you for being quite clear on that issue, and I think in the name of all the Judges here, thank you. Mr. Kehoe, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, we can take a look at these, a series of documents. We can go through these quickly. I believe, Mr. Registrar, they're in chronological order. Mr. President, it might be easier and quicker if we just deal with all of these documents at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Each time you speak of going faster, Mr. Kehoe, I feel elated so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, as long as I don't have you falling asleep yet in mid afternoon, I figure that's a success.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 616, 617A, 618, 618A, 619, and 620A. Each of the documents has an "A" version in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, take a look at all these documents. As with the previous document, these are again various documents, responses, requests, requests for assistance, a note to a commander, and they are all drafted by Mr. Dujmovic, and he also signs for them on your behalf, doesn't he, every one of those documents?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and all the documents came into being after my assistant was killed, Mr. Marko Prskalo, after the 17th of April, 1994, when Marko Prskalo -- I'm sorry, he wasn't killed, he was wounded by BH army snipers in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, take a look at that first document that you have, Exhibit 616. The date for that is 3 May, 1993. Now, these documents, General, run from -- and I'm talking about 615 -- run from the 30th of April till mid May of 1993. So during this period of time, Mr. Dujmovic did, in fact, have the authority to sign on your behalf; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dujmovic, throughout this period, was an officer in the IPD department, not an assistant for IPD, and such a situation may have occurred only after the assistant for IPD, Mr. Marko Prskalo, was wounded, but in reality what happened was that my assistants and the chiefs of staff signed on my behalf and not officers in departments, but the situation was such that there were only seven of us in the command as of the 16th of April, Prskalo was wounded, he was lying in hospital in the church at Nova Bila, and probably for that brief period of time, Dujmovic may have signed documents of this kind, requests, instructions, and other correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let's look at 620, and that is a request to the U.N. command dated 18 May, 1993. Did Dujmovic sign that on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Dujmovic signed that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he sign all of these documents on your behalf and with your approval?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He did sign all these documents that you have shown me, but I said already the circumstances, that is, when my assistant was wounded and he was unable to perform his duties. I was familiar with some of these events and I was aware of these developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's turn our attention back to 456/112, Mr. Registrar, the document that we were speaking about at the outset, which is the document that was sent to Mr. Thebault and that was signed by Mr. Dujmovic on your behalf. Now, when you told this Court, General, back on the 12th of April, 1999, with respect to this argument, that "Dujmovic never held such a position that would authorise him to sign any document on my behalf," that wasn't true, was it, because he did have authorisation to sign on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He did not hold a position -- when I say "position," I mean his official post. Officially, he was always an officer for IPD, he never was my immediate assistant; and according to the rules on the work of the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, he did not have such a position in the command which would give him the right to use my signature. I am talking about the position he held according to the formal structure of the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you have these internal regulations, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I've never seen them, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges would need to have these regulations which specify these responsibilities. Continue, Mr. Kehoe. So this is a question that the Judges will have to pose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, despite your answers to Mr. Nobilo's questions, there were times when Mr. Drago Dujmovic was authorised to sign for you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He did so, but he didn't have an official position to authorise him to do that. If Mr. Dujmovic had acted responsibly, he should have given all those documents to me to sign, because I repeat, he was just an officer, a clerk, and they had no right of signature, no right to sign such documents. If I was present, I had to sign them; if I was absent, then my chief of staff or the next deputy, and it is quite common knowledge who that person is in the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Were you absent on the 3rd and the 18th of May to sign these documents? Were you absent?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would have to look it up in the chronology of events, but I assume that I wasn't absent, that I was in the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us assume that you were not there. You have someone who doesn't hold an official position, according to what you say, according to your internal rules which we have never seen, he had no right to sign, and you have just told us that, generally speaking, you do accept responsibility for everything that bears your stamp. Then I assume that you cannot be satisfied when you learn of somebody writing to the Red Cross, the British Battalion, the 3rd Corps, to UNHCR of Zenica, to the UNPROFOR command, et cetera, when you see this, you cannot be pleased. So that means that your zone is not functioning properly. You must have been angry. You would have to dismiss him, take sanctions against him, 616 to 620. You yourself said that everything bearing your stamp, you are responsible for, but now you are telling us he didn't have the right. I don't know. If somebody tomorrow signs decisions of the Chamber in my name, I certainly wouldn't be pleased with it. But you must explain this to us. You must give us a precise answer to the questions of the Prosecutor. The Judges need these answers. You consider yourself responsible for everything bearing your stamp. I am going too fast. I'm sorry. You consider yourself responsible for everything bearing your stamp. We have documents for a period of 15 days, from 616 to 620, signed by Mr. Dujmovic. Do you consider yourself responsible or not for these documents signed by Mr. Dujmovic? Let us be very precise about this.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not agree with such acts by my associates. I did take steps. I cannot tell you specifically what exactly I did at what point in time, but I do know that I demanded all my associates to be very careful as to who was authorised to sign and who was not, and the general rule was that if I was present in the command, I would sign; if not, the document would wait for me to sign it. But the circumstances under which we operated were such that there were very often certain omissions made, and I consider this to be an omission on the part of my associate, Mr. Dujmovic, because those documents should have been signed by me if I had been present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When you are present with Mr. Valenta and Mr. Kostroman, do you consider yourself responsible for what they say? So I don't know -- I am changing my subject, yes, but I am pursuing my own logic, Mr. Hayman. Your presence, from the standpoint of presence, when we have these documents here, your client is telling us "if I was present." So he is setting a large number of conditions. "I consider myself responsible if I was present. If I see the assistant draft a letter, sign it in my name, and in that case, I am responsible." Or is it the interpretation that is wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, there may have been an error in the interpretation. The client answered clearly that Dujmovic did not have the position authorising him to sign and that he made a mistake but that he accepts all the documents emanating from the command as his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Kehoe, and thank you, Mr. Nobilo. It's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, did you know that Dujmovic was signing all these documents on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did know and learn later about this omission on the part of Dujmovic, and I'm sure that I discussed this matter both with Dujmovic and his superior later on, Mr. Dragan Ramljak and that we did undertake certain steps. Whether it was a reprimand or a disciplinary measure or counselling, but I am quite sure that I did discuss this with Dujmovic and caution him, telling him that he did not have a position giving him the right to sign documents on my behalf. But I wish to underline once again that these are events linked to the conflicts in Travnik and there were very few of my associates present whereas, at the same time, fighting was very intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the bottom line, General, is that these documents were signed by Dujmovic on your behalf and you approve their contents; is that your testimony to the president?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we have the documents specified, which ones he's talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Talking now 615 to 620.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may cast a glance through them, of course, Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know -- we're about to just change subjects a little bit. The General can review these at a break, if you would like to take a break at this juncture, and I can come back and ask him that question and he can answer that question and we won't waste any time while he's reviewing them to the extent that he needs additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, as suggested by the Prosecutor, we will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, the question we left off with with regard to documents 615 through 620 were these documents that were signed by Drago Dujmovic. Is it your testimony that you now say that you have authorised those particular documents and their contents? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As regards these documents, I claim that they all bear the registration number 01 and that according to the rules it was my duty to sign those documents. Drago Dujmovic acted correctly in drafting those documents, but he made a mistake in signing them. The rule was for me to sign them all and only exceptionally, if I'm unable to do so and the documents are urgent, only then could they have been signed by my assistants, the chief of staff, and other authorised persons. Drago Dujmovic had no such authority. I have reviewed the contents of these documents, and I support the contents of the documents from 615 through 620. I would have signed those same documents, and I believe that the associates authorised to do so would have done so if I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, General Blaskic. That is clear now. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let us now turn our attention back to 456/112, your 26 May, 1993 letter to Mr. Thebault. Now, General, this is again the document that we discussed before that was signed by Mr. Drago Dujmovic. Now, do you authorise the contents of this document, and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that this too is a document 01-5-68-9, therefore, a document that I was authorised to sign. Drago Dujmovic did not have the position authorising him to sign it on my behalf. A document of this content was something that I did not approve of, because I feel that the document contains certain elements which concerned the political figures representing the Croats, and the Bosniak Muslims, and particularly the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said in your direct examination, this is at page 20175, line 9: "I had quite a number of meetings with Mr. Thebault but never did I discuss with him any political issues because that was not my duty, nor did I have any such competence. If I had known of this document," and we're referring to 456/112, "If I had known of this document, I never would have approved it or approved it being sent to this address." Do you stand by that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I stand by that testimony that I spoke with Mr. Thebault most frequently about military issues. Those were the topics of our conversations. I always made it clear to him that if he wanted to discuss political matters with me or the functioning of the civilian authorities, that I was not the competent person but, rather, the representatives of the civilian authorities in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn our attention to another document, General, and it is the document in sequence right above this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is document 621, 621A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, looking at this document again, General, this is again a document that was signed by -- or drafted by Drago Dujmovic and signed by Drago Dujmovic on your behalf; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It is a document written and signed on my behalf, but let me just review the document for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is not a French copy, General, so I will read it briefly. It is a brief document. It is the 26th of May, 1993, 1810, to ICRC Zenica: "Request for additional engagement. "Since representatives of both the military and political leadership of the Croatian and Muslim peoples have officially agreed on the organisation of provinces number 8, 9, and 10 according to the Vance-Owen Plan and since this anticipates the organisation and functioning of normal life, we ask you to again mediate with representatives of 3rd Corps command to fulfil their obligations and release Croats who are in prison. "We stress that the following prisons, the Zenica House of Correction, the Bilmiste Secondary School, the Secondary Music School, the Students' Dormitory, the Old Age Pensioners, and the Kindergarten in Travnicka Street, hold a large number of Croats who are being detained for no justifiable reason. "We have released all detainees who were on territories controlled by the HVO. The realisation of this proposal would rebuild trust among the people and facilitate the future implementation of agreements." General, this, as you can see in the number sequence, is one number after 456/112 and I'm looking at your registration number 01-5-68-9/93 and that's the Exhibit 156/112, and the new Exhibit 621 is one up, 01-5-690/93. Now, sir, with regard to 621, this new document, again it talks about the implementation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Would you have authorised and did you authorise the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we look at the document, 456/112 was issued at 1800 and this one at 1810. Document 621 was issued at 1810. So this document is headed "Request", addressed to the International Red Cross. If I was in a position to study this document before signing it, I certainly would not have put this preamble in connection with the Vance-Owen Plan, but the request for the release of prisoners is something I support. I wish to underline that in this case too, Mr. Dujmovic clearly acted in an unauthorised manner. He committed an administrative error. I would have changed this document. I would have kept the request for the release of prisoners, that is, the second and third paragraph. However, the first paragraph I would not have sent to the International Red Cross because it isn't even important for the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, why -- General, who signed this document? We're talking about Exhibit 621.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Document 621 was signed, without any authorisation, by Mr. Dujmovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony is that you would never have authorised the letter to Mr. Thebault, 456/112, and you never would have included paragraph one on Exhibit 621; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would not have approved, in this overall context, the content of the letter to Mr. Thebault. That is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, General. Before I do that, let me ask you a question, General. You noted for us, both on direct and cross-examination, and I ask you to take a look first at Exhibit 456/112, you noted both in response to questions by Mr. Nobilo and this afternoon that you had never spoken to Mr. Thebault about politics, and "If I had known about this document," Exhibit 456/112, "I would never have approved it or approved it being sent to Mr. Thebault." My question for you, General, is: Is that testimony by you as truthful as everything else that you have told these Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Objection as to form, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Please rephrase the question. It is not a correct way to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the testimony that you gave these Judges about not authorising this document, 456/112, was that truthful testimony, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Mr. Kehoe, that the witness is under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So all he says is truthful, unless you can show that he is lying under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 622.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have an extra copy for the witness, Mr. Usher, if it's necessary. You can give him a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could the document be read to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will take the document through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The question on the table at this point is: Is that the witness's signature?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature, but the document is in English before me so that I -- and as I don't understand English, I don't know the contents of that particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You, however, have signed it in its English version; haven't you? I seem to understand that you had under your orders a team of translators who were as efficient as ours. Wasn't that the case, General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't have such competent translators. I just had one, and he functioned as a translator/interpreter and as other things as well. I would have been lucky had I had the kind of interpreters that we have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, and thank you for our translators. I see that it is necessary to read this document again. The witness has signed it but cannot remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before I begin to read it, I want you to compare the reference number on 456/112, that you maintain that you didn't authorise, with the reference number on this Exhibit 622, and I think you'll agree with me that the reference numbers are the same, 01-5-689/93; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the numbers are the same here. It's written down in pencil, but the numbers are the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a document, Mr. President and Your Honours, to the European Monitoring Mission, and I might add, Mr. President, that this document that I'm reading, Prosecutor's Exhibit 622, was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by the Croatian side of the Ministry of Defence of the Federation. "European Community Monitoring Mission. Deliver personally to Mr. Jean-Pierre Thebault. "Respected Sir: "I beg you to make some more efforts and use your influence in persuading the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina 3rd Corps Command in realising the agreements made. "It is well-known by now that the high level representatives of Croat and Muslim people have militarily and politically agreed on implementing the Vance-Owen Plan in Provinces 8, 9, and 10. "The postponement of these activities have as a consequence people's suffering, destroying of goods and property as well as increasing the problems of how to organise normal life. Please make the 3rd Corps Command aware of the consequences and responsibilities that they will have to take for obstructing the realisation of what we agreed upon. "I suggest that you initiate a joint meeting that would help us define the possible problems in question." Now, General, that particular English version, in substance, is exactly the same as the B/C/S version that was signed by Drago Dujmovic that you say you neither approved nor would have sent had you known about it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and I assume and believe that Drago Dujmovic, after having written and signed the document, handed it in to be translated to the translator and that it arrived in front of me in this version, but, unfortunately, I was not able to read it, because I would always either sign the document or put my initials to it at the top if I read it and had given it thought because the original Croatian version was written by Drago Dujmovic and signed by him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next document, General. While you are looking at this document, General, I would ask you also to take a look at Exhibit 621.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I come back to what you've just said. Wouldn't it have been simpler for you to write in your own mother tongue and wouldn't it have been simpler for Mr. Thebault to have your letter translated by his own translators? We'll ask Mr. Thebault, if it's necessary to ask him that question, but I'm sure he had interpreters and translators working for him, because you found yourself in a very paradoxical situation, it seems. On the 26th of May of 1993, you end up signing a document which is written in a language you do not understand, a letter written by an assistant whose official functions you do not recognise, an assistant about whom you tell us that he's been writing letters for a month, he's been writing things that he shouldn't have written. Isn't it a very complicated system to put in place? Wouldn't it have been simpler for you to write in B/C/S and Mr. Thebault would have managed to have the letter translated; what do you think about this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, it would have been better had I been in a position to read the Croatian version of the document and then to send a document of that kind to Mr. Thebault. But, Mr. President, Mr. Dujmovic had the authorisation to compile documents and to draft them, but it was his duty to bring me the document for me to look at because he never had the authorisation to sign it and he violated the regulations and signed documents and then handed them over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand very well. But on May 26th, when you signed this document, and knowing what Mr. Dujmovic is capable of doing, it seems to me that if there is one document about which I would have felt that I shouldn't sign it because it was written in English, it is this one. If there is one document you should not have signed, it is this one. However, you chose to sign it.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know, but those were the circumstances. The situation was such that I endeavoured to send new documents to Mr. Thebault as soon as possible. As far as I know, he had one or perhaps two translators. But in any event, Drago Dujmovic here I believe sent the document to be translated and I had the English version before me to sign it, and I would have authorised the document, document number 456/112, and I would not have authorised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can I understand you, General? You had 456/112 in B/C/S before you that was signed by Drago Dujmovic and you also had Exhibit 622 in English which you signed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not say that, and that is not correct. That is not what I said. I said, Your Honours, that Drago Dujmovic took and wrote the document, document 456/112, and he made an administrative error by signing it. He was not in a position to sign it. I believe that he then handed the document to an assistant to have it translated, and the document -- I got the English version of the document to sign, which I then signed, without having in mind and before me the contents of the document, that is to say, 456/112, written and signed by Drago Dujmovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, General, that Exhibit 622, the document that you signed in English to Ambassador Thebault, you signed without knowing the contents of this document? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Think hard about this particular question, Mr. Blaskic. Did you sign this document without knowing what it was actually saying?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was certainly not informed of all the details and completely informed of the contents of the document, document 456/112. Perhaps I just had a rough idea in one or two sentences of what it was about because I didn't sign only one document, I had many documents, perhaps twenty documents, to sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We were talking about document 622, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. The letter to Ambassador Thebault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You signed this document written in English when, in fact, you did not understand what the document was saying; is that really what happened? You have to tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that I received rough information as to the contents of the letter but that I was not informed fully of the contents in full as I would have been able to do if I had been able to read it out in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you knew, generally speaking, what the document was talking about?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Generally, globally speaking, yes. Globally speaking, generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So globally speaking, you knew that you were sending this letter to Mr. Jean-Pierre Thebault and you were talking about implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is possible that that's what was said to me, and I assume that I was told it was about the military aspect of the Vance-Owen Plan or a meeting, the need for a meeting with the 3rd Corps. But all the details contained in document 456/112, I was not informed because I personally did not have a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you may continue -- oh, sorry. Of course. Judge Rodrigues has a question first. This is a very crucial point because we don't understand very well what you chose to sign, what you chose not to sign, what you did understand and what you did not understand. It is very complicated for us. You have to help the Judges. When do you have authority, when do you authorise a document, when do you not? I want to see through this. Judge Rodrigues will help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I hope I can help you, Mr. President, by asking that question. General Blaskic, if we look at this document, we see it is written in English. Even if I don't understand Croatian, if I read a document written in Croatian and if I see the words "Vance-Owen," "Provinces 8, 9, and 10," if I have a phobia, a political phobia -- forgive me for using this term -- I at once understand that the words "Vance-Owen" and "Provinces 8, 9, and 10" have to be taken out of the document. Am I right in thinking in that particular way? You don't understand English, but I think that names do not change, whether the text be written in Croatian or in English.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour, and I was informed, linked to the Vance-Owen Plan, that we had military aspects to perform, demobilisation, and that we had to have talks with regard to its implementation, if the plan were to be signed by the Muslim and Bosniak representatives, and in that sense, therefore, if there were questions related to the military aspects of the plan, I have no phobia about it and wouldn't run from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All right. General, just a second. Now, if you look at this document that is written in English -- have a look at it now -- by looking at the document, you are able to read the words "Vance-Owen Plan" and you are also able to read the words "Provinces No. 8, 9, and 10." So I think it is the same whether you are reading a text written in English or a text written in Croatian. It is possible to identify these words "Vance-Owen Plan" and "Provinces No. 8, 9, and 10" whether the text be in Croatian or in English.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible to identify those plans, to recognise the words "Vance-Owen Plan" and "Provinces 8, 9, and 10."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen has a question for you, General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, I want to read the first paragraph of this letter and to ask you whether this was something that you might have said. The first paragraph says: "I beg you to make some more efforts and use your influence in persuading the ABiH 3rd Corps Command in realising the agreements made." Was that something you might have said?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is something that I might have said because there was an agreement as to the joint command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, of course, that is something that I would have said. I'm thinking of the military agreement reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now I turn to the second paragraph. It reads: "It is well-known by now that high-level representatives of Croat and Muslim people have militarily and politically agreed on implementing the Vance-Owen Plan in Provinces No. 8, 9, and 10." Was that something that you might have said?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You didn't know about the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did know about the Vance-Owen Plan, but I also knew that the Muslim leadership signed the plan under certain conditions which they posed linked to maps, as far as I recall. There were some conditions that they posed. So that there was not a full agreement reached on the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. Had I written "Provinces 8, 9, and 10," then I believe that I would have written down 1, 3, and 5 as well, that is to say, the remaining provinces where, according to that Vance-Owen Plan, military units of the HVO were subordinate to the BH army units, where that was allowed, and in that sense, with this military portion of the Vance-Owen -- treatment of the Vance-Owen Plan, I would not agree, if I were at all to refer to the Vance-Owen Plan in the military respect, but I would not write about political matters in this part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So the error which you say existed in this paragraph was in its reference to a political agreement. I'm trying to grasp exactly what you consider to be the error in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I consider to be an error the fact that a military command refers, as it does in this document, to an agreement, a political agreement reached between the Muslims and the representatives of the Croatian people and in the military part as well because I do not know that an agreement of this kind had been reached as it is stated in this assertion here, speaking about the fact that the organisation of Provinces 8, 9, and 10 were concerned. What happened to Provinces 1, 3, and 5? And, generally speaking, I consider that political agreements need not be raised in documents of this kind, and in the document, I would refer to an agreement between the chief of the HVO main staff and the commander of the command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you have two problems with that paragraph. One, its reference to a political agreement and, two, its non-reference to certain other provinces.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, although looking at it in general terms, no other provinces are mentioned except for provinces 8, 9, and 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If you were writing it in Croatian, you would have specified some other provinces as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Had I written this document, I would have referred to the military agreement between the chief of the main staff of the HVO and the commander of the staff of the BH army linked to the formation of joint armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the remainder of the text?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do, linked to the observation which stipulates, that is to say, the next paragraph, that a lateness in activities, along the implementation of this plan and it probably means the Vance-Owen Plan, that people are suffering and everything else that is quoted there. I'd once again like to refer to the agreement on a cease-fire, which was signed on the 20th of April and 28th of April between the commanders of the two armies, General Petkovic and General Halilovic, and I would seek for the firm implementation of those agreements on a cease-fire, on the formation of a joint command and joint armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that the reference to people suffering should have been linked to the non-implementation of certain military agreements as well. Do I follow you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise that the Vance-Owen Plan was itself inherently political in nature?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I personally find it difficult to delineate and differentiate between how far it was political and how far it was of a state nature, because it implied the internal structure of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and having it divided up into provinces, as I understood it. This implied demilitarisation for those provinces and it also implied something linked to principles of freedom of movement and some other matters as well. But generally it was a rather expansive plan which included elements of politics, and state structure, and military matters as well, but I don't know the details well enough. I do know the ones linked to military matters, as far as I have been informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you, in your position, find it possible to separate the military aspects of the Vance-Owen Plan from the political aspects or would you have said that they both constituted an integrated and inseparable package?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that the political aspect must have come before all the other aspects, all the other agreements and everything else for it to be implemented, all the more so as there were many plans that were signed. With the Washington agreements, we saw that once politics had agreed, just as with the Dayton Accords, that the army then went before politics and very quickly implemented its part of the obligations undertaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I follow you, General. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, would you agree with me that this letter to Ambassador Thebault is, as the President Judge Jorda discussed, to a very senior Ambassador of the European Monitoring Mission? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This letter, 622, was addressed to Mr. Thebault, and I'm sure that it was dispatched to Ambassador Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: This letter to Ambassador Thebault is an extremely important letter; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it is a letter, we could say an important letter, but as I've already said, had I had an insight into it and had I been in a situation to do so, I would have changed certain portions of the letter. I quote the meeting with the 3rd Corps commander, not only from Ambassador Thebault but from Colonel Duncan as well, and the liaison officer in BritBat, and everybody I was able to come into contact with. I wanted to have a meeting with the 3rd Corps commander and to try to decide upon the implementation of the cease-fire. Unfortunately, these demands did not bear fruit and I did not have occasion to meet him for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador Thebault was the senior European representative in Central Bosnia as part of the European Monitoring Mission, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ambassador Thebault was head of the European Monitoring Mission, and he had a large number of meetings with me, as the head of the European Monitors for the Zenica region. I don't know exactly which area the monitoring mission covered but I know he was based in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, General, that you signed a letter to this rather powerful person without fully knowing the contents of that letter? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that I have already said that I signed this document, and I also described the circumstances under which I signed it. Unfortunately, I didn't read all the details of this document, but I believe that I was familiar with the overall content of the document but not the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, when you told Mr. Nobilo and this Court back on the 12th of April that if you had known of this document, "I never would have approved it or approve it being sent to this address," when you told this Court that in response to Mr. Nobilo's questions, that wasn't true, was it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is true, because even now I would leave out this paragraph that I have already mentioned in answer to a question by His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen. I would have left out that paragraph and have changed the contents if I had been in a position to authorise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, isn't it true that the only reason, only reason that you're acknowledging your participation in this document at all is because we showed you your signature on an English copy of that document? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that is not the only reason, what you are saying. I have already said that there were quite a number of initiatives on my part, and that I had asked for a meeting with Mr. Thebault so that he could mediate a meeting with the 3rd Corps for me. But I underline once again that my associate was not in a position to sign it. If he had shown is to me and if I was able to read it in the way it is written, I certainly would not have approved it. I would have changed its content. I would have changed the content of this document for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you ask or instruct your associate to draft a letter for you or did he initiate the drafting himself on his own and then bring the letter to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, Your Honour, how this letter came about but it is possible that I asked the document to be drafted and for him to draft it, but it is quite certain that I never approved his signing that document because, as I have already said, his position did not authorise him to do so, but the circumstances under which the document was drafted I'm not sure of now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You didn't think that he should sign it, you thought that you should sign it. Why was that? Was it because of your assessment of the importance of the letter?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The rule was -- there were rules which we drafted and prepared in the command of the Operative Zone regarding official correspondence. All documents bearing registration number 01 were signed by me. Only exceptionally, when I was absent, could this be done by my deputy, the chief of staff, Franjo Nakic but, again, the documents would wait for me, for me to review them to see what he signed on my behalf. So there were regulations, internal regulations in the command of the Operative Zone, because this document bears the code 01 and this is my code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What was the reason behind the rule that documents bearing serial number 01 had to be signed by you? Was it because of the importance of that category of documents?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the reasons -- that was one of the reasons, but we took over the earlier rules headed "Official Correspondence and Office Procedures" from the former JNA, and we adjusted those regulations to our own conditions, so that we said that all documents carrying the serial number 01 would be mine and only I would be authorised to sign them, and only exceptionally, when I was absent and the document was urgent, someone else could sign it who was authorised to do so on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Who would decide on whether a particular document would bear the serial number 01?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, mostly outgoing documents reflecting the positions of the command would be given that serial number. In the general affairs department, there was a list or instructions, and an officer in that general affairs department would mark documents that were within my sphere of responsibility in this way. The head of operations would categorise those documents, the documents that were for me, those for the chief of staff, for logistics, for information and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before a short break, Judge Rodrigues has something to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I think I heard you say that you didn't sign the documents because you were not available. There was a reason why the other person signed a document instead of you. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There were times when the document was extremely urgent and when an authorised person would sign the document instead of me, but these were exceptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But, General Blaskic, as you can see, the document 456 and document 622 have the same date and the same hour. Why were you there to sign document 622 and you were not there to sign document 456, because they bear the same date, the 26th of May, 1993, at 1800?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe, and I can check during the break, that I was in the command on the 26th of May, but I can check from my chronology, at this hour. So I could have signed this document too, but unfortunately, my assistant, Mr. Drago Dujmovic, who under no circumstances held such a rank, such a command position to be able to sign a document instead of me, he made this error and signed the document without showing it to me, giving me a chance to read it, authorise it, and sign it. Then I assume he gave this document to be translated, and then a pile of documents reached me, including this one which I signed, without looking through it in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, General, but you told Judge Shahabuddeen that you had at least two problems with document 622. Perhaps you're going to have a third problem. How could you sign a document if you were not in the command building? Maybe it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Listen, I think there were many questions. You can see that the Judges are perplexed regarding this problem of signature and your authority. I think that the interpreters will appreciate a quarter of an hour's break, after which we will work for another quarter of an hour or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President, Your Honours? If we can turn our attention, General and Mr. Registrar, to Exhibit 623? I don't know if the witness has got a copy of that. Oh, there it is. Thank you, Mr. Usher. Mr. Usher, if the witness can also be given Prosecution Exhibit 621 as well? As with the prior document, Mr. President, Your Honours, both 622 and 623 are documents that were provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by the Federation, Ministry of Defence, and this came from the Croatian side of the Federation, Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, do you have 623 before you, General? I realise that it's in English, but do you have that document before you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have document 623 in English before me, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to compare the reference numbers on both 621 and 623, and I think you will agree with me that the reference numbers are the same, 01-5-690/93; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the numbers are the same and, obviously, document 623 was a translation of document 621.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, the signature on the bottom of 623 is yours, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the signature is mine on the English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this again is a document that was signed in the B/C/S version by Mr. Dujmovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct, and I checked in my chronology of events and I could answer the question posed to me by the Judge a moment ago.
