Mr. Dujmovic did sign the document although, as I've already said, he had no authorisation to do so, but I was at the command at the time, I had a meeting with Colonel Duncan on that particular day, and I asked him, that Colonel Duncan should mediate for a meeting with the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army to discuss the implementation of the military agreement that had been reached. Therefore, I asked Colonel Duncan and Mr. Thebault and the other officials to act as go-betweens and to help me organise a meeting with the 3rd Corps commander to avoid further conflict and to effect the implementation of the military agreement and agreements signed by our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this document, 623, is a document that's sent to another important international organisation, the ICRC or the International Committee of the Red Cross; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted during the course of your testimony, on 621, that you would not have approved paragraph 1 of that document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the style in which the first paragraph was written, I would have changed the style of the first paragraph, and we'll refer to the military agreement signed between my own chief of the main staff and the commander of the staff of the BH army, so that portion which relates to the approach, and I would change that in paragraph 1 had I been given the document to look through and had I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, you had a chance to look at this document, did you not, both in the B/C/S, before you signed it, and English, didn't you, or did someone force you to sign this in English before you had a chance to read it in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, nobody forced me to sign it and I was basically told what the document was about and I believe that the head of the operative section, I think he must have told me roughly what the document was about, if it was a request for a meeting or a request for the freeing of prisoners. But I repeat, that is to say, that had Mr. Drago Dujmovic acted correctly once he had written the document, he would come to me, have handed the document for me to scrutinise and sign, and I would then have entered my corrections into paragraph 1 and I would have signed the rest and the document would then be far clearer to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, as Judge Rodrigues asked you with the prior document, this document, in paragraph 1, references the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and Provinces 8, 9, and 10, and you can see that even in the English version, can't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that, and those parts are mentioned in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and the provinces involved in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, as Judge Rodrigues noted, is a very political matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is a state, political, and military question because each one of those provinces included many problems which had to be solved within the frameworks of the structure of the state within Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the tasks of the army, as indeed each plan provides for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, the political problems in those provinces were very significant to you, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Political problems were significant, but I did not work on them and I don't consider myself to be responsible for those political issues. I was interested in the military aspects of the Vance-Owen Plan, and if the plan was signed by all parties, what my responsibilities were as a military commander, what I had to do. That is how I viewed the plan, the military aspects of the plan. The political aspects of the plan were aspects that the political representatives were in charge of, those representing the Croatian and Bosniak people, and they were responsible to those very people, as indeed the implementation of any peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then it is clear, General, that during this period of time the Bosnian Croats wanted the Vance-Owen Plan to come into effect; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the political representatives of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina signed, as far as I know, all the plans offered by the international mediators. From the first plan -- I might be wrong, was it the Lisbon plan or some other plan? -- right up until this latest Dayton Plan, Dayton Agreement, so they signed absolutely all the plans that existed which the International Community offered, as far as I know, from official information received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at this plan that you're referencing in these documents. Mr. Registrar, if we could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 20, the first map on the top of Prosecutor's Exhibit 20. And just take a look at the provinces that we're talking about here, 8, 9, and 10. Prosecutor's 20. It is a small map, yes. We can just put it on the ELMO. That's it. We're talking about the top map, if we can, Mr. Usher, which is first iteration of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, 2 January, 1993. If we can blow that a little closer, please? If we can get those numbers? That's good. That's good. Thank you very much. Now, General, as we can see from this particular document, the areas of interest to you, Provinces 8, 9, and 10, were the areas that basically touched upon the Central Bosnian Operative Zone; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't see very well yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about that --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me look at the plan, please. That's better. Now I can see it better. Would you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly. The areas that you are mentioning in these letters, both to the International Red Cross and to Ambassador Thebault, are the Vance-Owen Provinces 8, 9, and 10, and those are of concern to you because those three provinces impact in some way on the Central Bosnian Operative Zone; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it is not only them that impact on the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. I testified that the greatest problem for me in the Vance-Owen Plan was and what I feared was demobilisation and disarmament of an army which had not been organised, structured, or armed. However, the Vance-Owen Plan, as I understood it, and that can be seen from this particular map, includes Province 7, Sarajevo, where Kiseljak, the municipality which I come from, and Kresevo and other areas, they were to be within the composition of Sarajevo, as well as a large portion of the 3rd operative group of Central Bosnia, that is to say, Zepce, Maglaj, Usora, which should have been under the command of the 3rd Corps. So this Vance-Owen Plan, looking at it territorially speaking, does not only incorporate the Central Bosnia zone but the 3rd Corps of the BH army as well as the areas under the 4th Corps of the BH army and the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the 2nd Corps of the BH army, that is, there were a large number of units in 1993 there, about 200.000 soldiers from the BH army in the area, the area that we're discussing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for reference purposes, Your Honours, the two blue areas 8, and 9, and 3 were areas designated to go to the Croats. For the purposes of this documentation, the prior testimony from Mr. Donia province 9 was due to go to the Muslims. So 3, 8, and 10 were due to go to the Croats, and 9, for the purposes of this discussion, were supposed to go to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We also had province 7, Sarajevo, with the district including Kiseljak and Kresevo within the composition of the Sarajevo district, as far as I know. So province 7 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us look at the letter, 623, that you signed to the International Red Cross. It is in English, so I'll read you a paragraph that you do not agree with. Again, this is a request for additional engagement and reads as follows: "The high level representatives of Croat and Muslim people have officially agreed, both militarily and politically, to implement the Vance-Owen Plan in provinces numbered 8, 9, and 10, which is the imperative for arranging a living more secure and normal than it is now." The balance of this letter talks about the freeing of Croats from various gaols in Zenica. Now, General, again, is it your testimony that this letter that is sent to the International Committee of the Red Cross in Zenica and was signed by you was neither read by you nor were you fully aware of its contents? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I claim that I was not informed with the original part of the document, of document 621, and that I had not read it, that I did not have occasion to read it, and it was signed by my clerk, Mr. Drago Dujmovic. The request sent to the Red Cross, I support it and stand behind it, except for the style and approach and the description of the agreements relating to the Vance-Owen Plan and other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How can you talk about style, General Blaskic? You say, "I stand behind it except in terms of style." How can you judge style if you don't understand the document? It's a very subtle comment that you just made. In order to be able to judge style you must be able to read the letter.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I say that I didn't have occasion to read the letter and that I did not agree with the details from the first portion of the letter, first part of the letter. Globally speaking, I agree with the part relating to the request made to the International Red Cross to mediate in these matters. I claim that my assistant -- had my assistant done what he should have done, he would have brought me the entire letter for me to look at and sign. I don't know why he didn't, because on the 26th of May I was at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This very subtle distinction you have just introduced between what's military and what's political, it is a very subtle one, I have to underscore that, but that is something you have said, is it something you think the people you sent these letters to had this distinction in mind? When you sent this to Mr. Thebault, does he answer you, "Well, General Blaskic, we see you as a military man of the team and not as the politician of the team, so stick to military matters and do not meddle with politics"? I had the impression that you were seen as a man capable of writing such a letter. Nobody ever told you -- well, I'm rephrasing my question. Has anybody told you one day, "Well, Mr. Blaskic, for us you are the military man. You're not a politician. So don't bother about this. Why are you meddling with this?" Have you ever heard such a thing?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Thebault endeavoured, at our meetings and during our talks, and asked of me for my observations on political problems and civilian matters, and sometimes he would present his views. He never said outright, "I do not ask you to expound on political problems for me." But I told him at meetings, whenever questions of this kind arose, I said, "Mr. Thebault, those are questions for the civilian representatives and the political representatives, and you can discuss those matters with them. I cannot discuss those questions because I do not consider myself competent." If anybody asked me for my personal opinion, perhaps there were discussions of this kind where we shared our personal opinions, but I told him that I myself was not competent to discuss political or civilian matters, and I said this not only to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We know what was happening between yourself and your assistant. We know what was happening between yourself and the people you sent these letters to. Now, let's see what was happening between you and your superiors. Did they one day tell you, "Don't write this. Don't ever write that document again because this is not what you're supposed to do." Did General Petkovic say one day -- well, I'm sure he understood English. Did he one day tell you, "Well, this is not admissible what you've just written in this paragraph"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I was appointed command of the Operative Zone I was told that, "Politics is not your business. Leave politics to the politicians. It is your duty to deal with military problems and matters." That is how I understood my duties and that is what General Petkovic led me to conclude through the orders he issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, as far as the Vance-Owen Plan is concerned, it was a very subtle distinction. Any questions from the other Judges? No. Very well then. Is this document something that you're finished with, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one last question on these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, the bottom line is that you signed two letters to two international agencies where you discussed a very political matter, the Vance-Owen Plan; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is true that I signed the two translations, that is to say, the two versions in English, and that I did not sign two versions in the Croatian language because my assistant did not submit the document to me for scrutiny. It is true that I would have changed things in both letters had I been able to do that. I think that it was an administrative error on the part of the man who signed the documents on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions on these documents, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you to the interpreters. They've had a very hard day. Thank you to the court reporters as well. We'll meet again tomorrow morning at 10.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
